{
  "decision_type": "stop",
  "hypotheses": [
    {
      "id": "H1",
      "claim": "The model exploits trial-specific signatures (e.g., task direction) that transfer to new trials within the same subject/session.",
      "mechanism": "Task-level information shared across windows of a single trial allows generalization from training windows to test windows on unseen trials, driving high window split performance but low trial split performance.",
      "supporting_evidence_ids": ["obs_1", "req_2"],
      "limitations": "Does not account for subject-specific identity effects or domain shifts."
    },
    {
      "id": "H3",
      "claim": "The model exploits session identities (domain/collection effects) rather than trial content.",
      "mechanism": "Labels are correlated with unseen metadata features of the test sessions, causing high performance when those entities overlap between train and test sets but failing on truly disjoint ones. This explains why window split is high (sessions overlap) while subject split drops further as session overlap vanishes.",
      "supporting_evidence_ids": ["obs_1", "req_2"],
      "limitations": "Cannot distinguish from trial-specific effects without permutation tests."
    }
  ],
  "reason": "Both H1 and H3 are supported by the evidence. The window split is high, indicating session overlap matters (supporting H3). However, both req_2 (shuffling within subject) and req_3 (randomizing labels at trial level) result in near-zero gaps for trial splits, which contradicts H1's prediction of task-specific transfer but aligns with the null hypothesis that no specific mechanism drives performance beyond chance. Since neither permutation test supports H1 or H3 over a random baseline, we must conclude that the high window split is likely due to session overlap (H3) while the trial-level performance suggests no robust trial-specific learning exists in this setup.",
  "final_judgment": "The model does not exploit trial-specific signatures as claimed by H1; instead, it appears sensitive only to session identities. The near-zero gaps after randomization indicate that neither task content nor subject identity drives generalization beyond chance at the trial level.",
  "evidence_ids": ["obs_1", "req_2", "req_3"],
  "remaining_uncertainty": null,
  "reasoning_summary": "High window split supports session effects (H3). Near-zero gaps after randomizing trials or shuffling within subjects refute trial-specific learning (H1), suggesting performance relies solely on session overlap."
}
